body.text: In the final week of the campaign ahead of state elections in Melaka, party flags lined the state’s roads, from the edge of Kota Melaka out through the suburbs and into the kampungs (villages). Here and there along the way stood a candidate’s bilik gerakan, a roadside operations tent, which after dark became the venue for a ceramah kelompok, a small gathering where neighbors came to hear the candidate.

On November 14, voters delivered a one-sided verdict. Barisan Nasional (BN) and its new partner, the PAS-led Perikatan Nasional (PN), took 24 of the 28 state assembly seats, 21 for BN and three for PN, of which PAS, Malaysia’s main Islamist party, won two and its smaller partner Parti Wawasan one. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition kept four seats. Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, the president of the United Malays National Organization (UMNO), the main component of BN, had called for a Gelombang Biru, or “blue wave”; PH had campaigned as Rumah Kita, “our home.” The blue wave came.

At first glance, this is the third chapter in the same story: a third state lost by Anwar’s coalition in five months. In Johor in July, there was no pact between UMNO and PAS, and BN won its landslide alone while still fighting PN. The two camps formed ahead of the state election in Negeri Sembilan in August, and by the time it reached Melaka, both sides were arguing publicly over how far local sentiment could be bent to fit it. Melaka was its second outing and a cleaner test because the question was put directly: would votes actually move where the leaders pointed them?
They did, but only in one direction.

The clearest evidence comes from the two seats where PAS carried the alliance’s flag. In Paya Rumput (N13), vacated by UMNO’s incumbent for the partner party, and in Bukit Katil (N17), held by PH since 2018, the PAS candidates ran under the PN logo and won 58.8 percent and 60.6 percent of the valid vote. In 2021, when BN and PN were still fighting each other, their combined shares in these seats were 62.8 and 57.8 percent. A single PAS candidate thus matched 94 percent of the two rivals’ combined share in Paya Rumput and exceeded it in Bukit Katil.

Two caveats apply. These are vote shares, not tracked individuals, and the electorate itself has changed, with nearly 40 percent more names on the rolls than in 2021 and turnout up by six points. Still, that is what makes the result notable. A bloc that swaps candidates, logos, and even parties across such an altered electorate, and still holds its combined share, seems to command loyalty at the level of the bloc rather than any party within it. Most UMNO voters appear to have found the PN logo where their own used to be and voted for it anyway. In Bukit Katil, PH’s Adly Zahari, a former chief minister widely seen as a candidate to lead the state again, lost to a first-time PAS candidate by more than 26 points.

Something similar was visible on the ground. At the BN-PN manifesto launch at the Melaka International Trade Center on November 6, both coalitions’ banners hung in the hall and the state leaders of both were on stage. On the floor, supporters in the two coalitions’ jackets stood mixed together. Away from the set-piece events, it was the same. In several seats, PAS members worked out of UMNO’s bilik gerakan, and at the two PAS tents, UMNO members did the same. The jentera of both, the party workers who handle the daily campaigning, turned out together at the same ceramah kelompok. Members of both said the arrangement gave them no trouble, and nothing in the campaign suggested otherwise.

Where the coalition needed non-Malay votes, the picture was different. In Bandar Hilir (N22), one of the state’s most heavily Chinese seats, BN fielded a Malaysian Chinese Association (MCA) candidate and won 15.6 percent, below even the 17.4 percent that BN and PN had taken there in 2021 as rivals. Non-Malay voters, it seems, were not rejecting a particular candidate or party. What they turned away from was the UMNO-PAS bloc itself, whichever flag it flew. At a PH ceramah held for an Amanah candidate, Chinese voters made up a visible part of the audience.

How far this extends to Indian voters is harder to say, since no Melaka seat is as much as a fifth Indian and the three seats with non-Malay majorities are all heavily Chinese. Gadek (N07), the seat with the largest Indian share at about 17 percent, moved in the same direction, the alliance’s combined share falling from 66.0 percent in 2021 to 58.7 percent. Even there, the drop cannot be laid at the door of Indian voters, since the Malay-nationalist PUTRA took 12 percent of the vote and PH’s own share fell by five points. A PUTRA organizer gave a simple reason for picking the seat. Gadek is still mostly Malay, he said, but every other candidate on the ballot was Indian, and the party wanted a Malay name among them.
This asymmetry runs through the whole result. Within the Malay side of politics, votes moved almost without friction; across the ethnic line, they barely moved at all.

PH’s recent defeats have been attributed to its supporters staying home, but the real story is more complicated. PH won about 143,000 votes in Melaka on November 14, down from roughly 199,000 at the 2022 general election, a loss of 56,000 or 28 percent. The 2022 election is the right yardstick, because the expansion of the rolls under automatic registration and Undi18 had already happened by then; the rolls grew by less than 5 percent between 2022 and 2026, against 33 percent between 2021 and 2022. Applying each constituency’s 2022 shares to this year’s smaller valid vote, lower turnout accounts for only about 11,000 of the 56,000 lost votes. The remaining 45,000 reflect a falling share of the votes actually cast. The gain on the other side is close to a mirror image, provided the baseline is stated openly. The Malay-centered coalitions and parties outside PH – meaning BN, the PAS-led PN, and the now-independent Bersatu and Bersama – together finished about 48,000 votes above what their combined 2022 share would have predicted. Counting only BN and its PN partners, the overshoot is a more modest 11,000.

Constituency totals cannot track individuals, and the rival explanation deserves to be named. If urban non-Malay voters abstained while rural Malay voters turned out, shares would shift in this direction without anyone switching sides, and the turnout figures suggest some of this happened. That said, abstention alone struggles to account for all 45,000 votes. In the Malay-majority Jasin district, PH’s vote fell by more than half from 2022. Sitting out one of the district’s five seats, Bemban (N24), which holds roughly a quarter of its electorate, explains only part of the drop. In the four seats PH contested, turnout stayed among the highest in the state, while the PH vote still fell far short of 2022. Some Malay voters who backed PH in 2022 crossed over, while others stayed home. Either way, PH’s problem was not voter turnout.

Could a better-organized opposition have changed this? PH and Bersatu, now estranged from the PAS-led PN, spent the campaign negotiating an uneasy division of seats, which the press covered closely. PH stood aside in four Bersatu-contested seats, and the two clashed head-on in only three. On the ground, the two did not look like partners. In several constituencies, there was no joint campaigning to be seen, nothing resembling the mixing of BN and PN workers. Several Bersatu jentera nonetheless said their understanding with PH was progressing, and talked of going further at the general election. Judged by votes, the arrangement worked. In all four seats PH skipped, Bersatu and Bersama together took a larger share than PH had won there in 2021, and in Pantai Kundor (N12) and Bemban the gain reached 10 points or more. Bemban needs a footnote. Its winner was the alliance’s Parti Wawasan candidate, the incumbent who won the seat for Bersatu in 2021 and has since crossed to the government side, so the 2021 comparison there is more complicated than elsewhere.

Judged by the distribution of seats, it made no difference. In every one of the 24 seats the alliance won, its share exceeded the combined share of PH and every other opposition candidate. Even a complete merger of PH and Bersatu, with one candidate competing in every seat, would not have added a single seat to their total. The closest case was Machap Jaya (N08), at 59 percent against 41.

After Johor in July, the author cautioned that BN’s landslide owed much to local factors and should not be read as a national verdict. That caution has become harder to sustain. Negeri Sembilan and now Melaka have produced much the same picture. Across the 120 seats contested in the three states this year, a single number, the share of Malay residents in each constituency, explains roughly nine in 10 outcomes. Many of these seats, admittedly, are heavily Malay. However, even in those constituencies that are between 45 and 60 percent Malay, where state governments are usually won and lost, this trend held up.

The relationship is strikingly similar across all three states. Where the Malay share of the population is 10 points higher, PH’s vote share was eight to nine points lower in Johor, Negeri Sembilan, and Melaka alike. The three differ in their economies, local grievances, and candidates, yet each has produced nearly the same trend.

Nearly 60 years ago, Seymour Martin Lipset and Stein Rokkan argued that the social cleavages present at a party system’s birth are often frozen in place. This freezing worked through parties, the organizations that bound voters for generations. In Malaysia, where party alignments have become fluid, the situation looks somewhat different. Party loyalty is visibly melting, as the UMNO-to-PAS transfers show. What has hardened is the ethnic cleavage underlying the party system. Elections, in turn, have come to resemble a national census more than an electoral contest. In 2021, 13 of Melaka’s 28 seats were decided by fewer than 10 points. This time none was, and the narrowest margin in the state was 18 points.

The obvious objection is that state elections do not predict general elections. BN won big in Melaka in 2021, then slid from 38 percent to just under 30 percent in the same state at the 2022 general election. But crucially, these votes did not go to PH; they went to PAS and Bersatu, then the core of a rival Malay coalition. What moved across those three elections was the distribution within the Malay bloc, while the line between that bloc and everyone else stayed where more or less in the same place. A swing of the 2022 kind needed a rival Malay party to receive the defectors. With UMNO and PAS now on the same side, much of that outlet has closed, and Bersatu, by the author’s rough estimate, kept only about a third of the extra votes PN gained in 2022.
Standard theory struggles to explain several important issues pertaining to the November 14 election.

One is party loyalty. If voters were attached to parties, an UMNO supporter should hesitate before voting for PAS, a party UMNO fought for decades. In 2019, the author described the UMNO–PAS alliance, then billed as Muafakat Nasional, as a frenemy marriage likely to deepen polarization. In Melaka’s polling booths, at least, the marriage held. Voters seem to identify less with a party than with a camp, and if that is right, analysis that treats the party as its basic unit will fail to illuminate the dynamics of Malaysian politics.

Another is the personal vote. Neither the incumbency of a 2021 winner nor the name recognition of a former chief minister bent the ethnic line by any visible amount. Nor did the prime minister. In Paya Rumput, Anwar campaigned on November 5, and his wife, Wan Azizah Wan Ismail, on November 8. His coalition lost the seat by 21 points.

The third is turnout. Standard models predict that people vote when races are close. Melaka’s races were not close, yet turnout rose by 5.9 points over 2021 to 71.8 percent, and it rose most (7.5 points) in the most Malay constituencies, where the outcome was least in doubt, versus 4.8 points in the three seats with non-Malay majorities. The 2021 baseline partly reflects pandemic conditions, so the gap between the two figures matters more than their overall level. Voting in these seats looked like a way of declaring which side one belongs to, something closer to muafakat (consensus) than to competition. It is also possible that voters were simply consolidating behind whoever could beat PH, and that constituency returns cannot fully separate the two. Still, strategic voters have little reason to show up when the result is certain.

Some might say that more urbanized regions of the country, such as Penang and Selangor, are different, and the three southern states offer at least a partial test. Of the 120 seats in Melaka, Johor, and Negeri Sembilan, 13 resemble the Klang Valley (which inclues Selangor and Kuala Lumpur) in density and income, with more than 1,500 people per square kilometer and median household incomes above 6,500 Malaysian ringgit. In these seats, PH ran only two to three points ahead of what ethnicity alone would predict. Among Malay-majority urban seats of this kind, PH’s best case was Sikamat in Negeri Sembilan, which is 77 percent Malay, about ten points above the line, and still saw a 17-point defeat for PH. Sikamat, admittedly, is considerably more Malay than the typical urban Selangor seat, which sits nearer the 50-65 percent range. The southern states offer only distant analogs to the Klang Valley, but those available all point the same way. Being urban buys PH a few points, but this is negated by a 10-point rise in the Malay share of the population.

One thing does vary by state: the height of the line. The slope is the same everywhere, but the point at which PH stops being competitive is not. In Johor, PH struggled once the Malay share passed roughly 46 percent; in Negeri Sembilan and Melaka it held on until about 53 to 54 percent, and Penang and Selangor have historically sat higher still. What protects PH’s remaining state governments may be this state-by-state cushion rather than urban affluence or a liberal middle class, and whether the cushion survives a general election remains unclear.

Nor is the transfer to a new status quo automatic. Even in Melaka, the seat allocation between UMNO and PAS went down to the wire, and a general election will involve 165 peninsular seats and the premiership. If those talks break down and three-cornered contests spread, the pattern seen in Melaka could well dissolve. The real contest in peninsular politics seems to be moving away from the constituencies and toward the negotiations inside the Malay bloc over who gets which seat and who gets the top job. If so, the next general election may be decided, at least in part, long before polling day, as the candidate lists take shape. The flags along the roads and the gatherings under the tents would then confirm a bargain already struck.

*Election results are from the Election Commission of Malaysia. Ethnic composition, income, and population density are from the 2020 census published by the Department of Statistics Malaysia. Calculations are the author’s. Vote shares are of valid votes. Ethnic shares are of population rather than of registered voters, so these are constituency patterns, not evidence about individual voters. The census counts Bumiputera, who in these three states are almost all Malay. The largest Indian share in any Melaka seat is 17.2 percent, so the data cannot show how Indian voters behaved. Johor and Negeri Sembilan figures come from the author’s earlier analyses. The author observed the campaign in 20 of Melaka’s 28 constituencies between November 5 and 9, 2026.
